item.title: Electron Configurations, Coulombic Attraction, and Sodium Ionization
item.stimulus:
A chemistry class is studying how electron configurations and Coulomb's law explain the behavior of atoms and ions. The class collected the following data from reference tables.

Quantity | Value
Distance between ion centers in NaCl(s), Na+ to Cl− | 2.82 Å
Distance between ion centers in MgO(s), Mg2+ to O2− | 2.11 Å
First ionization energy of Na | 496 kJ/mol
Second ionization energy of Na | 4562 kJ/mol

Answer the following.
item.model_answer:
(a) Sulfur has 16 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴.

(b) Neutral Fe is [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶. Forming Fe3+ removes the two 4s electrons first and then one 3d electron, giving Fe3+ = [Ar] 3d⁵ (1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁵).

(c) F ∝ q1q2/r².
F(MgO)/F(NaCl) = [(2)(2)/(2.11 Å)²] / [(1)(1)/(2.82 Å)²] = 4 × (2.82/2.11)² = 4 × 1.786 = 7.14.
The attraction between Mg2+ and O2− is about 7.14 times as strong.

(d) Na is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s¹. The first ionization removes the single 3s valence electron. Na+ is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶, so the second ionization removes a 2p core electron. The 2p electron is in the n = 2 shell, much closer to the nucleus, and it is shielded only by the 1s electrons, so it experiences a much greater effective nuclear charge than the 3s electron, which is shielded by all ten core electrons. By Coulomb's law, the smaller distance and larger effective charge produce a much stronger attraction, so far more energy (4562 kJ/mol versus 496 kJ/mol) is needed to remove the second electron.
item.verification_python:
import math
# (a) S electrons
s_config=[2,2,6,2,4]
assert sum(s_config)==16
# (b) Fe3+ electrons: Fe has 26, Fe3+ has 23; [Ar]=18 plus 3d5
assert 26-3==18+5
# (c) Coulomb ratio
r_nacl=2.82; r_mgo=2.11
ratio=(2*2/r_mgo**2)/(1*1/r_nacl**2)
assert abs(ratio-7.14)<0.01
assert abs((r_nacl/r_mgo)**2-1.786)<0.001
assert round(ratio,2)==7.14
# (d) Na configs
na=[2,2,6,1]
assert sum(na)==11
assert sum(na[:3])==10
assert 4562>496
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

parts.prompt: Write the complete ground-state electron configuration (no noble-gas shorthand) of a neutral sulfur atom, S.

criteria.evidence: Response gives 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁴, with 16 electrons placed in Aufbau order.
criteria.fix: Count the atomic number to get total electrons, then fill subshells in Aufbau order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p.

parts.prompt: Write the ground-state electron configuration of the iron(III) ion, Fe3+. Noble-gas shorthand is acceptable. Indicate which subshells the removed electrons came from.

criteria.text: Correct configuration of Fe3+: [Ar] 3d⁵, with the two 4s electrons and one 3d electron removed
criteria.evidence: Response gives [Ar] 3d⁵ (or 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁵) and states that the 4s electrons are removed before a 3d electron.
criteria.fix: For transition-metal cations, remove electrons from the highest-n subshell (4s) first, then from 3d.

parts.prompt: Using Coulomb's law and the data in the table, calculate the ratio of the magnitude of the attractive force between Mg2+ and O2− in MgO to that between Na+ and Cl− in NaCl, treating the ions as point charges.

criteria.text: Correct force ratio F(MgO)/F(NaCl) = 7.14 with supporting setup
criteria.evidence: Response sets up F ∝ q1q2/r², uses charge product 4 (2 × 2) for MgO and 1 for NaCl with the given distances, and reports about 7.14 (7.1 also accepted).
criteria.fix: Write F ∝ q1q2/r² for each pair, divide the two expressions, and square the distance ratio before multiplying by the charge ratio.

parts.prompt: The second ionization energy of Na is much greater than its first ionization energy. Identify the subshell from which each electron is removed, and explain the large difference in terms of Coulombic attraction.

criteria.text: Identifies that the first electron is removed from the 3s subshell and the second from the 2p subshell
criteria.evidence: Response states that the first ionization removes the 3s valence electron and the second removes a 2p core electron.
criteria.fix: Write the configuration of Na and Na+, then note which subshell loses an electron at each step.

criteria.text: Explains that the 2p electron is closer to the nucleus and less shielded (greater effective nuclear charge), so Coulombic attraction is much stronger
criteria.evidence: Response connects the larger second ionization energy to the 2p electron being in a lower shell (n = 2), smaller distance from the nucleus, and experiencing less shielding or greater effective nuclear charge, giving a stronger attraction per Coulomb's law.
criteria.fix: Explain ionization energy using both distance from the nucleus and shielding, linking each to the strength of Coulombic attraction.

item.title: Electron Configurations and Coulombic Attraction in F and Cl
item.stimulus:
Fluorine (atomic number 9) and chlorine (atomic number 17) are both in Group 17 of the periodic table. A student uses a simple Coulombic model in which the outermost electron of each atom is attracted by an effective nuclear charge, Zeff, at an average distance r from the nucleus. The model values are given in the table below.

Atom | Subshell of outermost electron | Zeff | r (pm)
F | 2p | +5.10 | 64
Cl | 3p | +6.12 | 99

The Coulombic force between two charged particles is given by F ∝ q1q2/r².
item.model_answer:
(a) Cl: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁵. Cl⁻: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ (the added electron completes the 3p subshell).

(b) A Cl atom has 10 core electrons (1s² 2s² 2p⁶) and 7 valence electrons, located in the 3s and 3p subshells (3s² 3p⁵).

(c) F ∝ Zeff/r² because the electron charge is the same in both atoms.
F atom: 5.10/(64)² = 5.10/4096 = 1.245 × 10⁻³
Cl atom: 6.12/(99)² = 6.12/9801 = 6.244 × 10⁻⁴
Ratio = (1.245 × 10⁻³)/(6.244 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.99 ≈ 2.0
The force on the outermost electron in F is about 2.0 times the force in Cl.

(d) F has the greater first ionization energy. The outermost electron of F is in the 2p subshell (n = 2), while that of Cl is in the 3p subshell (n = 3), so the F electron is much closer to the nucleus (64 pm versus 99 pm). By Coulomb's law the force depends on 1/r², so even though Cl has a slightly larger effective nuclear charge, the attraction on the F electron is about twice as strong. A more strongly attracted electron requires more energy to remove, so the first ionization energy of F is greater.
item.verification_python:
import math
ZF, rF = 5.10, 64
ZCl, rCl = 6.12, 99
fF = ZF/rF**2
fCl = ZCl/rCl**2
assert abs(rF**2-4096)<1e-9 and abs(rCl**2-9801)<1e-9
assert abs(fF-1.245e-3)<1e-6
assert abs(fCl-6.244e-4)<1e-6
ratio = fF/fCl
assert abs(ratio-1.99)<0.01
assert round(ratio,1)==2.0
# electron counts for Cl
config = [('1s',2),('2s',2),('2p',6),('3s',2),('3p',5)]
assert sum(n for _,n in config)==17
core = sum(n for s,n in config if s[0] in '12')
val = sum(n for s,n in config if s[0]=='3')
assert core==10 and val==7
ion = config[:-1]+[('3p',6)]
assert sum(n for _,n in ion)==18
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

criteria.evidence: Both configurations are written correctly, with the added electron placed in the 3p subshell for Cl⁻.
criteria.fix: Fill subshells in Aufbau order for 17 electrons, then add the extra electron of an anion to the lowest available subshell, here 3p.

parts.prompt: State the number of core electrons and the number of valence electrons in a neutral chlorine atom, and identify the subshells that hold the valence electrons.

criteria.text: 10 core electrons and 7 valence electrons, with the valence electrons in the 3s and 3p subshells
criteria.evidence: Response gives 10 core and 7 valence electrons and identifies 3s and 3p (the n = 3 shell) as the valence subshells.
criteria.fix: Count electrons in the outermost shell (highest n) as valence; all electrons in lower shells are core electrons.

parts.prompt: Using the model values in the table, calculate the ratio of the Coulombic force on the outermost electron in F to the Coulombic force on the outermost electron in Cl. Report your answer with the correct number of significant digits.

criteria.evidence: Shows the Zeff/r² setup for each atom (electron charge cancels) and reports a ratio of about 2.0 (2 significant digits, limited by r).
criteria.fix: Write F ∝ Zeff/r² for each atom, divide the two expressions, square each distance, and round to the fewest significant digits in the data.

parts.prompt: Predict which atom, F or Cl, has the greater first ionization energy. Justify your prediction using Coulomb's law and the electron configurations of the atoms.

criteria.text: F has the greater first ionization energy because its outermost electron is in the n = 2 shell, closer to the nucleus, so it is attracted more strongly
criteria.evidence: Claims F is greater and justifies with Coulomb's law: the 2p electron of F is at a smaller distance (fewer shells) than the 3p electron of Cl, so the attractive force is larger (about twice as large) despite the slightly smaller Zeff, requiring more energy to remove.
criteria.fix: Compare shell number (distance) and effective nuclear charge, then argue that a larger Coulombic attraction means more energy is needed to remove the electron.

item.title: Electron Configurations and Coulombic Attraction in Iron Ions
item.stimulus:
Iron (atomic number 26) forms two common oxides, FeO and Fe2O3. FeO contains Fe2+ ions and Fe2O3 contains Fe3+ ions. In each oxide, every iron ion is attracted to neighboring oxide ions, O2−. The table gives approximate center-to-center distances between an iron ion and an adjacent oxide ion.

Ion pair | Charge on iron ion | Charge on oxide ion | Distance between ion centers
Fe2+ and O2− | +2 | −2 | 2.16 × 10² pm
Fe3+ and O2− | +3 | −2 | 2.00 × 10² pm
item.model_answer:
(a) Fe has 26 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 3d⁶ (or [Ar] 4s² 3d⁶).

(b) Fe3+ has 23 electrons: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁵ (or [Ar] 3d⁵). The two 4s electrons are removed first because n = 4 is the outermost shell, and then one electron is removed from the 3d subshell.

(c) More energy is required to remove an electron from Fe3+. In Fe the electron removed is a 4s electron, in the n = 4 shell, farther from the nucleus. In Fe3+ the electron removed is a 3d electron in the n = 3 shell, which is closer to the nucleus. Also, Fe3+ has 26 protons attracting only 23 electrons, so there is less electron–electron repulsion and a greater effective nuclear charge on each electron. By Coulomb's law, F ∝ q1q2/r², a larger effective charge and a smaller distance produce a stronger attraction, so more energy is needed to remove the electron.

(d) F ∝ q1q2/r².
F(Fe3+–O2−) ∝ (3)(2)/(2.00 × 10² pm)² = 6/40000
F(Fe2+–O2−) ∝ (2)(2)/(2.16 × 10² pm)² = 4/46656
Ratio = (6/40000) ÷ (4/46656) = (6 × 46656)/(4 × 40000) = 1.75
The attraction in the Fe3+–O2− pair is 1.75 times as strong as in the Fe2+–O2− pair.
item.verification_python:
from fractions import Fraction
Z=26
fe=[('1s',2),('2s',2),('2p',6),('3s',2),('3p',6),('4s',2),('3d',6)]
assert sum(n for _,n in fe)==Z
fe3=[('1s',2),('2s',2),('2p',6),('3s',2),('3p',6),('3d',5)]
assert sum(n for _,n in fe3)==Z-3==23
r3=Fraction(200);r2=Fraction(216)
ratio=(Fraction(3*2)/r3**2)/(Fraction(2*2)/r2**2)
assert abs(float(ratio)-1.7496)<1e-4
assert round(float(ratio),2)==1.75
assert Fraction(6,40000)==Fraction(6)/r3**2
assert 216**2==46656
print('ALL_CHECKS_PASSED')

parts.prompt: Write the complete ground-state electron configuration of a neutral Fe atom.

criteria.evidence: Response gives all subshells with correct superscripts totaling 26 electrons, ending 4s² 3d⁶ (either listing order, or noble-gas shorthand).
criteria.fix: Fill subshells in Aufbau order 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d until the electron total equals the atomic number.

parts.prompt: Write the ground-state electron configuration of the Fe3+ ion, and identify the subshell(s) from which the three electrons were removed.

criteria.text: Fe3+ is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁵, with both 4s electrons removed before one 3d electron
criteria.evidence: Response gives a configuration with 23 electrons ending in 3d⁵ with no 4s electrons, and states that two electrons come from 4s and one from 3d.
criteria.fix: When forming transition-metal cations, remove electrons from the highest n shell (4s) before removing any 3d electrons.

parts.prompt: Claim whether more energy is required to remove one electron from a gaseous Fe atom or from a gaseous Fe3+ ion. Justify your claim using Coulomb's law and the electron configurations from parts (a) and (b).

criteria.text: Claim: removing an electron from Fe3+ requires more energy, justified by Coulombic attraction
criteria.evidence: Response states Fe3+ requires more energy and explains that the electron removed from Fe3+ is a 3d electron, closer to the nucleus than the 4s electron removed from Fe, and/or that Fe3+ has 26 protons attracting only 23 electrons (greater effective nuclear charge), so the attraction is stronger.
criteria.fix: Link ionization energy to Coulomb's law: compare the distance of the removed electron from the nucleus and the effective nuclear charge it experiences.

parts.prompt: Using Coulomb's law and the data in the table, calculate the ratio of the magnitude of the attractive force in the Fe3+–O2− pair to that in the Fe2+–O2− pair. Report your answer to the correct number of significant figures.

criteria.text: Ratio of forces = 1.75, obtained from F ∝ q1q2/r²
criteria.evidence: Response shows (3 × 2 / (2.00 × 10²)²) ÷ (2 × 2 / (2.16 × 10²)²) or equivalent and reports 1.75 (three significant figures).
criteria.fix: Write F ∝ q1q2/r² for each pair, divide the two expressions so constants cancel, and keep three significant figures from the distances.
